mainProgression.description: Classic country I-IV-V7 progression forming a 12-bar blues-influenced structure

sectionProgressions.progression: E - E - E - E | A - A - E - E | B7 - A - E - E
sectionProgressions.romanNumerals: I - I - I - I | IV - IV - I - I | V7 - IV - I - I
sectionProgressions.description: Modified 12-bar blues form adapted for country with the V7 chord providing dominant tension
Classic dominant-to-tonic resolution used at the end of each verse to propel into the next

harmonicFunction: E (I) - Strong tonic center establishing the key and home chord
A (IV) - Subdominant providing harmonic movement and contrast midway through each verse
B7 (V7) - Dominant seventh chord creating strong pull back to E with the D# leading tone
The 12-bar structure reflects the blues influence on early country and rockabilly
The V7-IV-I turnaround at the end of each verse is a hallmark of country-blues hybrid harmony

techniques.name: Boom-Chicka-Boom Train Rhythm
techniques.description: The signature Johnny Cash the iconic vocal hook that mimics the sound of a locomotive, with bass notes on beats 1 and 3 and muted strums on beats 2 and 4

notes: E: 0-2-2-1-0-0 (Open E major chord)
A: X-0-2-2-2-0 (Open A major chord)
B7: X-2-1-2-0-2 (Open B7 chord)
Beat 1: Strong bass note (root) played with downstroke on low strings
Beat 2: Muted 'chicka' strum - palm rests lightly on strings for percussive hit
Beat 3: Alternate bass note (5th) played with downstroke
Beat 4: Muted 'chicka' strum for the second percussive beat
The pattern creates the characteristic 'BOOM-chicka-BOOM-chicka' train sound
sequence: For E chord: bass on open low E (beat 1), chicka (beat 2), bass on B at 2nd fret A string (beat 3), chicka (beat 4)
For A chord: bass on open A (beat 1), chicka (beat 2), bass on E at 2nd fret D string (beat 3), chicka (beat 4)
For B7 chord: bass on B at 2nd fret A string (beat 1), chicka (beat 2), bass on F# at 2nd fret low E string (beat 3), chicka (beat 4)
Maintain the relentless train-like momentum throughout the entire song
tips: The train rhythm should feel mechanical and relentless like a locomotive
Keep palm contact light for muted strums - just enough to deaden the strings
The bass notes must be strong and clearly defined against the muted strums
Practice with a metronome to develop the steady driving pulse
Luther Perkins played this with just the bass strings and one or two treble strings
details.progression: E - A - E - B7 - E (Boom-Chicka-Boom Pattern)

techniques.name: Travis Picking Bass Lines
techniques.description: Alternating thumb bass pattern inspired by Merle Travis, providing a walking bass line underneath the boom-chicka rhythm

notes: Thumb alternates between root and 5th of each chord on beats 1 and 3
E chord bass walk: E (open 6th) - G# (4th fret 6th) - A (5th fret 6th) - B (2nd fret 5th)
A chord bass walk: A (open 5th) - B (2nd fret 5th) - C# (4th fret 5th) - E (2nd fret 4th)
B7 bass walk: B (2nd fret 5th) - C# (4th fret 5th) - D# (1st fret 4th) - E (2nd fret 4th)
The walking bass line connects chord changes smoothly
sequence: Start with simple root-fifth alternation on each chord
Add chromatic passing tones between root and fifth
Incorporate the walking bass line during chord transitions
Keep the right hand thumb independent from the fingers strumming treble strings
tips: Start by mastering the simple alternating bass before adding walking notes
Keep the thumb moving steadily regardless of what the fingers are doing
The walking bass should seamlessly connect one chord to the next
This technique requires patience - work on thumb independence daily
details.progression: E - A - E - B7 - E with walking bass connections

techniques.name: Country Lead Fills
techniques.description: Simple pentatonic-based fills between vocal phrases using bends and slides characteristic of early country guitar

notes: Based on E major pentatonic: E - F# - G# - B - C#
Primary fill positions around the 2nd and 4th frets (open position)
Uses hammer-ons from G to G# (open to 1st fret on G string)
Characteristic country bend on G string 1st fret (half-step bend)
Keep fills sparse and rhythmic, fitting between vocal lines
sequence: Wait for vocal phrase to end before playing fill
Start fill from a chord tone of the current chord
Use two to four notes maximum per fill
Resolve the fill before the next vocal phrase begins
tips: Less is more - Luther Perkins was famous for his sparse, effective fills
Keep fills rhythmically aligned with the boom-chicka pattern
Use the open E and B strings as pedal tones during fills
Practice fills separately before integrating with the rhythm
details.progression: Over E - A - E - B7 - E progression

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: The song opens immediately with the driving train rhythm on E major, establishing the locomotive groove
notes: Establishes the iconic train rhythm immediately
Luther Perkins' electric guitar sets the groove
Bass and drums lock into the boom-chicka pattern
The relentless pulse mimics the rhythm of a moving train

sections.name: Verse 1
sections.description: First verse with the 12-bar structure, E for four bars, A for two bars, back to E, then B7-A-E turnaround
sections.progression: E - E - A - E - B7 - E
notes: Follows a modified 12-bar blues structure
Maintain the train rhythm through all chord changes
The A chord provides subdominant lift in the middle
B7 to E turnaround propels into the next verse

sections.name: Verse 2
sections.description: Second verse continuing the 12-bar pattern with the same chord structure
sections.progression: E - E - A - E - B7 - E
notes: Same 12-bar structure as verse 1
Lead guitar fills become slightly more embellished
The vocal melody intensifies with the prison narrative
Rhythm remains locked and steady throughout

sections.name: Guitar Solo
sections.description: Instrumental break featuring Luther Perkins' sparse, iconic lead guitar work over the 12-bar structure
sections.progression: E - E - A - E - B7 - E
notes: Luther Perkins' signature sparse lead style
Uses E major pentatonic for melodic content
Simple but effective single-note lines
Maintains the train rhythm underneath the lead

sections.name: Final Verse & Outro
sections.description: Final verse building to the conclusion with a definitive E major ending
sections.progression: E - A - E - B7 - E (final resolution)
notes: Most intense vocal delivery of the song
the signature verse with powerful narrative
Final B7-E turnaround resolves the song definitively
Ends on a strong E major chord

alternatives: Any solid-body electric with single-coil pickups
guitar.pickup: Bridge single-coil for twangy, percussive country tone

settings.bass: 4 (controlled low end for tight bass notes)

effects.other: Slapback delay (80-130ms, single repeat) for authentic Sun Records/Tennessee Three tone

beginner.focus: Master the open E, A, and B7 chords and the basic boom-chicka train rhythm
steps: Learn open E, A, and B7 chord shapes
Practice the boom-chicka strum pattern on E chord alone
Add chord changes: E to A and E to B7
Play through the entire 12-bar verse structure at slow tempo (75 BPM)

intermediate.focus: Develop alternating bass technique and add simple lead fills between vocal phrases
steps: Master root-fifth alternating bass for E, A, and B7
Learn walking bass lines connecting chord changes
Add simple pentatonic fills in the spaces between phrases
Practice at performance tempo (112 BPM) with consistent groove

advanced.focus: Combine Travis picking bass with lead fills for solo guitar arrangement
steps: Integrate walking bass with boom-chicka rhythm simultaneously
Develop Luther Perkins-style lead guitar fills
Master the complete 12-bar structure with all embellishments
Perform the song as a solo guitar piece with bass, rhythm, and lead combined

commonMistakes: Losing the steady train rhythm when changing chords
Making the muted strums too loud relative to the bass notes
Rushing the tempo - the train rhythm must be steady and relentless
Overthinking the B7 chord change - keep it smooth and simple
Adding too many fills - Luther Perkins' genius was his restraint
practiceRoutine: Warm up with boom-chicka pattern on open E for 5 minutes
Practice E-A-E changes with boom-chicka at 80 BPM
Add B7 turnaround: B7-A-E pattern at slow tempo
Work through the full 12-bar form at gradually increasing tempos
Practice lead fills separately, then integrate at slow tempo
focusAreas: Clean chord transitions within the boom-chicka pattern
Alternating bass note accuracy on each chord
Muted strum technique for percussive 'chicka' sound
metronomeWork: Start boom-chicka pattern at 75 BPM on E chord
Add chord changes at 85 BPM through the 12-bar form
Build tempo to 100 BPM with clean transitions
Reach performance tempo of 112 BPM with consistent timing
